Rain taps against the window like a quiet code only the lonely understand. I watch it blur the streetlights into golden smears, turning the ordinary world outside into something softer, stranger. There’s a particular solitude in evenings like this—not sadness, exactly, but a hollowed-out calm, as if the rain has washed everything too loud or sharp away.  

I think about all the things we carry silently: the unsent texts, the names we still mouth in the dark, the dreams that shrink a little more each year to fit the shape of our practical lives. We edit ourselves constantly—to be palatable, employable, loved—but sometimes, in the hush of a rainy night, the unedited version leaks through. The one who’s tired. The one who’s afraid. The one who still believes, stubbornly, in magic.  

My coffee’s gone cold. The cat curls tighter into my lap, a warm comma in the sentence of this moment. Outside, a car hisses through a puddle, its headlights stretching long and liquid across the pavement. Someone’s heading home, or away—I wonder which feels more like relief tonight.  

Rain doesn’t care about our contradictions. It falls equally on rooftops and ruins, on gardens and gutters. Maybe that’s the lesson: to pour yourself out without asking if you’ll be enough. To trust that even the smallest drop changes the shape of the world, however briefly.  

The tap-tap-tap continues. I breathe. For now, this is enough.
